report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infection and a cause of adverse reproductive outcomes.
Epidemiologic studies describe bacterial vaginosis (BV) as a major risk factor for CT infection.
Emerging data suggest that BV-associated bacteria and their metabolites contribute to CT susceptibility.
Here, we measured the role of specific bacteria in incident CT and evaluated a hypothesized causal role between the vaginal microbiota, its metabolites, and CT risk.

We conducted a nested case-control study of Kenyan women who engage in transactional sex from the Mombasa Cohort who acquired CT versus those who did not, and compared their vaginal microbiome and metabolome at the visit preceding CT acquisition.
We determined CT infection and total bacterial load using qPCRs.
16S rRNA sequencing was used to characterize the genital microbiome, and BV status was determined using Nugent-Hillier and Amsel scoring criteria.
Metabolites were measured using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from a subset of women.
Findings: Women with BV, high vaginal microbial diversity, and community state types III and IV were significantly more likely to have CT at their next visit.
CT infection itself did not alter vaginal microbial diversity.

More specifically, both concentrations and relative abundances of Lactobacillus crispatus and several BV-associated bacteria (Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella/Prevotella timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum) were predictive of CT outcomes.
Vaginal metabolites differed between cases and controls pre-CT, including Tyramine, reduced and oxidized Glutathione, and sucrose.
In a mediation analysis, the vaginal metabolome significantly mediated the relationship between the microbiome and CT infection.
Interpretation: We show for the first time that the association between BV and CT risk is mediated by differences in the metabolome.
Identification of the mechanisms underlying increased CT risk with BV can inform interventions to reduce infections in high-risk women.
Evidence before this study: Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection globally and can lead to serious adverse health outcomes.
Previous studies have pointed to an association between the vaginal microbiota composition, particularly the presence of bacterial vaginosis (BV)-associated taxa, and chlamydia susceptibility.
However, most studies have been cross-sectional, measuring the microbiome at the time of infection.
The few longitudinal studies specifically assessing the microbiome dynamics preceding CT infection have generally been limited by small sample sizes or infrequent sampling.
Further, the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear.

Added value of this study: In this nested case-control study, we evaluated the vaginal microbiome preceding CT acquisition and compared participants who subsequently acquired infection with matched controls who remained uninfected.

We found that women who acquired CT had a significantly higher vaginal microbial diversity in the past 1-2 months, while the CT infection itself did not lead to broad changes in the microbiome, suggesting directionality to this relationship.
Participants who acquired CT were >2-fold more likely to have BV by Nugent-Hillier or Amsel criteria at the previous visit.
text.formatted: Participants who acquired CT were >2-fold more likely to have BV by Nugent-Hillier or Amsel criteria at the previous visit.

text.text: Having a diverse community state type IV was associated with the strongest likelihood of CT acquisition.

More specifically, women who acquired CT were more likely to have a microbiome characterized by the depletion of Lactobacillus crispatus and higher abundances of Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella (Prevotella) timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum.
To assess the possible mechanism through which the microbiome influenced CT risk, we measured the cervicovaginal metabolome in a subset of participants.
We found that 70% of the effect of the vaginal microbiome on CT acquisition risk could be explained by the metabolome, highlighting the role of bacterial metabolites in CT susceptibility.

Overall, by focusing on samples collected prior to infection acquisition, with a short period between visits, our study contributes robust temporal evidence that the vaginal microbiome impacts CT susceptibility rather than simply being correlated, with the presence of CT, with metabolites potentially playing a key role in this relationship.

Implications of all the available evidence: Our findings support the concept that the vaginal microbiome is a potentially modifiable risk factor for CT acquisition, with specific BV-associated bacteria, alongside L. crispatus depletion, identified as key modulators of risk.
This study is a step towards confirming the directionality of the microbiome-CT infection relationship and establishing potential mechanisms through which the microbiome influences CT risk.
These findings, along with previous literature, have the potential to lead to microbiome or metabolite-targeted interventions that would reduce the risk of CT acquisition.

With over 130 million infections globally each year, Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) is the most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) 1 , accounting for approximately 40% of all STIs 1.

text.text: Prevalence is highest among adolescent and reproductive-aged women and is linked to serious adverse health outcomes, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, neonatal infections, and increased risk for HIV acquisition 1 .

text.text: Preventing CT infection is a global public health priority.

Epidemiologic studies identify bacterial vaginosis (BV), classically characterized by a higher abundance of anaerobic and pathogenic bacteria such as Gardnerella, Fannyhesseae, and Prevotella species, amongst others, as a risk factor for CT infection 2, 3 .

text.text: A growing body of longitudinal and mechanistic studies points to the role of specific BV-associated bacterial taxa in CT acquisition, persistence, and clearance, while Lactobacillus species dominance, particularly L. crispatus, is protective [4] [5] [6] [7] .

text.text: In young women in the US, a diverse vaginal bacterial community with high relative abundances of Lachnocurva vaginae preceded CT acquisition 8 .

text.text: However, mechanisms driving this relationship are unknown.
BV-associated shifts in the vaginal metabolome may contribute to increased risk of CT.
Urogenital CT requires tryptophan for growth and to establish an infection, which it can salvage from indole, a metabolite produced by several BV-associated bacteria 9,10 .

More specifically, CT infection correlated with higher vaginal kynurenine/tryptophan ratios and diverse anaerobic microbiota, highlighting an immunometabolic link between microbiome composition and host susceptibility 10.
text.formatted: More specifically, CT infection correlated with higher vaginal kynurenine/tryptophan ratios and diverse anaerobic microbiota, highlighting an immunometabolic link between microbiome composition and host susceptibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref>.

text.text: Loss of Lactobacillus dominance corresponds with elevated pH, reduced lactic acid, and increased short-chain fatty acid production, factors associated with mucosal barrier disruption and altered innate immunity 11 .
text.formatted: Loss of Lactobacillus dominance corresponds with elevated pH, reduced lactic acid, and increased short-chain fatty acid production, factors associated with mucosal barrier disruption and altered innate immunity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that the cervicovaginal microbiome influences CT pathogenesis by shaping epithelial/immune readiness, nutrient availability, microbial competition, and local metabolite milieu.

To better understand the temporal dynamics between BV and CT, and explore the mechanisms underlying their interactions, we conducted a longitudinal case-control analysis among HIVseronegative Kenyan women engaged in sex work.
We examined the impact of BV, specific bacterial taxa, and their metabolic profiles on the risk of acquiring CT.
Participants in this nested case-control study were enrolled in the Mombasa Cohort, an open cohort in Kenya established in 1993.
Cohort characteristics, eligibility criteria, and study protocol have been described previously 12 .
text.formatted: Cohort characteristics, eligibility criteria, and study protocol have been described previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Briefly, eligible individuals were of female sex at birth, aged 18-50 years, lived in Mombasa, engaged in transactional sex, and provided informed consent.

This nested case-control sub-study used data collected between September 2010 and November 2021 (suspended from March-July 2020 due to the COVID pandemic) from non-pregnant, HIVseronegative participants.
Although gender identity was not assessed in the Mombasa cohort, it was assumed based on the study protocol that all participants identified as cisgender women.
Ethical approval was obtained from the ethical review committees at Kenyatta National Hospital (P197/04/2012) and the University of Washington (STUDY00000615).
Structured interviews and physical examinations were conducted at enrollment, collecting demographic, sexual behavior, contraceptive, and sexual history.
Participants were followed longitudinally, and during monthly follow-ups, sexual behavior, vaginal washing practices, and symptom data were collected.
Pelvic examinations and clinical and laboratory evaluations for STIs were performed.
Blood samples were collected monthly for HIV testing.

As part of the larger Mombasa Cohort study, vulvovaginal cotton-tipped swabs (Puritan, USA) were collected monthly for BV evaluation by Nugent and Hillier scoring, and nucleic acid amplification STI testing (NAAT) for CT, Neisseria gonorrhoea, and Trichomonas vaginalis.

Quarterly visit samples were tested for STIs by NAAT, and monthly swabs were tested for BV, vulvovaginal candidiasis, wet mount, and N. gonorrhea culture, while the other swabs were stored at -80°C. Syndromic management was used for STI treatment during study visits, with additional treatment provided based on laboratory test results.
Additional Dacron dry swabs (Puritan) were stored for multi-omic analyses.
Quarterly visit NAAT results were used to identify incident CT infections.
Once identified, stored monthly swabs were tested retrospectively to identify the first CT-positive visit (labeled as Index) and the preceding CT-negative visit (Index-1 visit).
These individuals were labeled as cases.
Incidencedensity sampling was used to randomly identify a set of matching control participants (CT-negative at two consecutive visits) at a 1:2 case: control ratio.
Overall, N=77 incident CT cases and N=154 controls were included from 166 unique individuals, of whom 45 contributed more than one distinct case or control sample pair across time (Fig 1).
text.formatted: Overall, N=77 incident CT cases and N=154 controls were included from 166 unique individuals, of whom 45 contributed more than one distinct case or control sample pair across time (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: BV testing: One vulvovaginal swab was smeared on a slide for a wet mount, which was used to diagnose BV using both the criteria of Nugent-Hillier and Amsel's criteria 13, 14 .
text.formatted: BV testing: One vulvovaginal swab was smeared on a slide for a wet mount, which was used to diagnose BV using both the criteria of Nugent-Hillier and Amsel's criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: Women were categorized as Nugent-Hillier BV-positive (scores 7-10), intermediate (4-6), or negative (0-3).

Women were considered Amsel BV-positive if they had three out of four criteria: vaginal pH>4•5, clue cells on wet mount, thin, homogeneous discharge, and a positive whiff test with 10% potassium hydroxide.
text.formatted: Women were considered Amsel BV-positive if they had three out of four criteria: vaginal pH>4•5, clue cells on wet mount, thin, homogeneous discharge, and a positive whiff test with 10% potassium hydroxide.

text.text: Bacterial community profiling using high-throughput 16S rRNA sequencing and total 16S qPCR: Stored swabs were thawed, resuspended in sterile PBS, and shaken at 100rpm for 3min.
Bacterial DNA was extracted using the Qiagen DNeasy Powersoil HTP 96 kit according to the manufacturer's instructions.
DNA was amplified using primers spanning the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene as previously described 15 .
text.formatted: DNA was amplified using primers spanning the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene as previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Amplicons were purified using AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter), quantitated using qPCR, and pooled in equal mass amounts.
Published mock communities of known abundance (BEI resources), and pure E. coli DH10B cultures were included as positive controls to be used in cross-contamination filtering and error rate modeling.

text.text: Multiple past studies have pointed to a link between CT infection and BV, but the causal relationship remained unclear, primarily as both are influenced by sexual behavior.
It is increasingly clear that behavioral factors are insufficient to explain the increased risk of CT acquisition and that biological factors are key.

In this cohort of Kenyan women at high risk for STIs, with frequent follow-up visits 12 , we show that acquiring a new CT infection was associated with significantly higher odds of having high vaginal microbial diversity in the past 1-2 months.
text.formatted: In this cohort of Kenyan women at high risk for STIs, with frequent follow-up visits <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> , we show that acquiring a new CT infection was associated with significantly higher odds of having high vaginal microbial diversity in the past 1-2 months.

text.text: The concentrations of specific taxa were strongly associated with subsequent CT acquisition.

Further, we demonstrate that CT acquisition does not change the overall microbiome composition, indicating a directional relationship where the vaginal microbiome at the time of CT exposure may be an important determinant of infection.
Finally, we found that the effect of the microbiota on CT acquisition may be mediated via its metabolome.

Two prior studies have examined the vaginal microbiome prior to incident CT, although these studies had longer periods of time between the prior and the incident visits (6-12 months) than in this current study.

In a cohort of young Dutch women, having an L. iners-dominant microbiota was associated with a 2•6-fold higher odds of acquiring CT within the year 19 , while a CST-IVA microbiota, but not CST-IVB or CST-III, was associated with a 2•51-fold increased odds of CT incidence among adolescents and young women six months before infection 8 .

text.text: Here, by measuring the odds of subsequent infection within 2 months, we can substantially advance our understanding of the direction of this relationship.

Along these lines, women were more likely to acquire CT if they had higher within-participant microbial diversity at the previous visit.
These increased odds appeared to be particularly associated with having a CST-IV microbial composition, with a >4-fold increase in CT incidence.

text.text: Furthermore, while women who acquired CT had a more diverse microbiome at baseline, the CT infection itself did not have an impact on the overall diversity, providing evidence that microbial diversity preceded infection.

The difference in microbial diversity between those who acquired CT compared to those who remained negative was driven by higher relative abundances of specific BV-associated bacteria, but to a larger degree, by the depletion in L. crispatus, where CT infection was preceded by a >2-fold lower relative abundance of L. crispatus.

text.text: The increased odds of CT acquisition were highest with increases in the abundances of P. amnii, H. timonensis and S. sanguinegens respectively, while the protective effect of L. crispatus was associated with 53% lower odds of infection.

The increases in these BV-associated taxa are like those described by Usyk et al (2025), who also report higher differential abundances of Prevotella and Sneathia spp., amongst others approximately 6 months before infection.
They did not report differences in Lactobacillus spp, although this may be due to the dynamic nature of the vaginal microbiota over time.
The fact that Prevotella spp. are strongly associated with risk raises the possibility that metabolites preferentially produced by this genus could enhance CT infectivity.
For example, Prevotella spp. have high sialidase activity 20 , which may facilitate CT infection.

text.text: In line with this, CT acquisition was associated with the presence of several metabolites at the preinfection visit.
Among those, GSH, GSSG, sucrose, glucose, G6P, GMP, guanosine, uridine, and NAD have previously been described as being associated with CT.
GSH may allow CT to remain infectious, while GSSG was involved in persistent infection 21, 22 .

The vaginal microbiome was highly predictive of the overall metabolome composition.

Importantly, 70% of the effect of the microbiome on CT risk was explained by the cervicovaginal metabolome, tying bacterial metabolites as the mechanism through which woman's risk of CT infection increases with BV.

text.text: A key strength of this study was its case-control study design, with short intervals between visits.
However, the small number of women with overlapping microbiome and metabolome data was an important limitation.

Nevertheless, our findings suggest that we show that the cervicovaginal microbial dysbiosis may play a substantive role in CT acquisition risk within the subsequent two months with taxon-specific influences and potentially mediated by microbial metabolites.
These findings may lead to interventions that could decrease risk of CT infection in women.
